item.content:encoded:
I recently got into virtual photography, which is taking photos inside video games. Editing my shots is what made me realize how little I understood about color, so I decided to dive into the topic with Claude and fill the gaps in my knowledge.

In my previous post, Exposure vs Brightness, Claude helped me measure and understand what the Exposure and Brightness sliders do to a pixel. Along the way I wrote that a pixel is three numbers from 0 to 255, and then added a throwaway line about a “Pandora’s box of color profiles and color spaces” that I couldn’t close again. This is me opening the box.

The question I should have asked first is a simple one: what does 255 · 0 · 0 actually mean? Everything below follows from it:

  • What is a color space? Is sRGB one? What does the “s” stand for?
  • Why can the same three numbers be two different colors?
  • If a screen can’t show a color, why not just use more bits?

Short version: RGB 255 · 0 · 0 is not a color. It’s an instruction (“turn the red light all the way up”), and which actual red you’ll see depends on the screen.

Disclaimer: I’m learning color by doing it, with Claude as my guide, so some of this may be wrong. I’ve marked what Claude explained to me and what we checked in code. If you spot a mistake, please tell me in the comments.

You can play with every number in this article. The small widgets do the real math, and Claude and I recomputed every number in the text in code, so nothing was just copied from a chat.

Key takeaways:

  • An RGB triple means nothing until you know its color space.
  • A color space is the contract that says what the numbers mean: which red, green and blue, which white, and how numbers turn into light.
  • A color profile is the label that says which color space is used. It’s a small file embedded in an image, or describing a screen.
  • A gamut is the colors you can mix from your three paints. On the map of visible color it’s a triangle, and a screen can’t leave it.
  • Same numbers, different color: sRGB red in P3 numbers is not 255 · 0 · 0.
  • More bits give finer steps, not new colors.

What is a color space? Why is it called sRGB?

Here’s where my mental model broke. I had always imagined 255 · 0 · 0 as “red”. But what you see depends on what the red light in your screen actually is. A color space is the contract that pins down what the numbers mean. It fixes three things:

  1. The primaries: exactly which red, green and blue, as measurable points. “Full red” means a specific, physical red. Picture the tiny red diode (subpixel) in your display: full red means that diode at full power, and it glows one particular red. Another display can have a slightly different red diode.
  2. The white point: what (1, 1, 1) looks like. White isn’t one fixed color. A sheet of paper looks warm under a candle and bluish in the shade, so a screen has to pick which white it means. Most spaces pick D65. It’s just the name of a standard white, roughly midday daylight. The “D” is for daylight, and the 65 is its color temperature, about 6500 K.
  3. The transfer function: how stored numbers map to amounts of light. This is the 2.2 “gamma” from Exposure vs Brightness: a stored 0.5 is only about 21% of the light, not 50%. I’m not going to repeat that here, but it is the third clause of the contract.

So “RGB” on its own is a family. sRGB, Display P3 and BT.2020 are members of it, each with specific values filled in.

The “s” in sRGB stands for standard. HP and Microsoft made it in the 90s, based on what typical monitors back then could show. HDTV uses the same primaries. Nearly everything on the web assumes it: an image with no color profile attached (more on profiles below) is treated as sRGB.

A map of color, and the triangles on it

Here’s the second thing that blew my mind. In 1931 scientists made a map of human vision. Plot every color a person can see on a flat chart, with brightness taken out, and you get a horseshoe-shaped region. For now just take it as a map.

Okay, but two things bugged me right away. Why is the horseshoe sitting exactly there? Why isn’t a corner at 0,0, and what are x and y even?

So I asked Claude. Turns out this map doesn’t use red, green and blue. It describes a color with 3 other numbers: brightness, and x and y. Fix the brightness at one level, draw only x and y, and you get the horseshoe. That’s also why it’s not like the RGB I’m used to, where 0,0 would be a corner. x and y aren’t “how much red” and “how much green”.

And how do x and y work, and why is there dead space outside the horseshoe? The high-level answer is above: the horseshoe is every color a person can see, so outside of it is stuff our eyes can’t see. But why it has this exact shape, and how x and y work? Magic for now. I want to understand it too, so we’ll dive in next time in Why the map of visible color is a horseshoe.

A screen mixes three lights. Any mix of three points lands inside the triangle they form.

Gamut. I first heard this word in Android talks (Romain Guy used it a lot, haha) and I pretended I understood it. Then I got into color, it was everywhere, and I was super confused. Finally, with the help of Claude, I got the real meaning (at least I hope).

Picture a paint box with three tubes: red, green and blue. Everything you can mix from them is the box’s gamut. A wide gamut doesn’t mean more tubes, it means stronger ones. A redder red, a greener green.

So a color space’s gamut is a triangle on this map. Here are the three I’ll keep mentioning:

Interactive illustration (gamut-chart). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

  • sRGB: the small triangle. The internet’s default, and what almost every screen can show.
  • Display P3: wider red and green. It comes from digital cinema and it’s what recent iPhones and Macs show.
  • BT.2020: red, green and blue corners almost on the edge of the horseshoe, because its primaries are single wavelengths of light. It was built for UHD and HDR video, and few displays reach all of it.

Claude helped me compute how much of the horseshoe each triangle covers: roughly a third for sRGB, almost half for Display P3 and about two thirds for BT.2020. You’ll see other figures online depending on how you measure, so treat these as ballpark.

For nerds: the exact primaries

These are the published values; I use them in the widgets. White is D65 at (0.3127, 0.3290) in all three.

Space Red (x, y) Green (x, y) Blue (x, y)
sRGB (0.640, 0.330) (0.300, 0.600) (0.150, 0.060)
Display P3 (0.680, 0.320) (0.265, 0.690) (0.150, 0.060)
BT.2020 (0.708, 0.292) (0.170, 0.797) (0.131, 0.046)

Same numbers, different color

This is where it gets practical. Take pure sRGB red, 255 · 0 · 0. Written in Display P3 numbers, it is #EA3323. And P3’s own 255 · 0 · 0 is a red that sRGB can’t show at all. It’s purer than sRGB’s red, so you’d have to take away a bit of green and blue to get there (negative green and blue), and you can’t have less than no light.

I got curious and asked Claude: why do we only talk about negative green and blue? Can’t the red go above 255 too? Turns out it can, P3’s red needs a bit more than full red. But that’s the easy problem. Dim everything a little and the red fits. Green and blue are stuck, because they’re already below zero and dimming doesn’t change that. So too much red is just too much brightness, and the negatives are what make the color impossible.

Back to the reds. The same three numbers really are two different colors:

Interactive illustration (srgb-vs-p3). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

If your screen is wide-gamut (most recent iPhones and Macs), the second swatch is visibly more vivid. If it isn’t, the widget tells you so, because there’s nothing to see.

This explains the “washed out” and “oversaturated” bugs everyone runs into when the color profile is wrong or missing:

  • sRGB numbers read as P3: every color gets stretched outward. Oversaturated, sunburnt skin.
  • P3 numbers read as sRGB: every color gets pulled inward. Dull and flat.

Here is what each one looks like. I took two of my own PS5 screenshots and, with the help of Claude, simulated the mix-up in code with the real sRGB and P3 numbers. It’s a simulation, not a screenshot of a broken app. In both pictures the left half is the correct one and the right half is the mix-up.

First, sRGB numbers read as P3:

Left: correct. Right: sRGB numbers read as P3.

The right side might look better at first glance, with its punchier colors. But it’s the wrong one. Those aren’t the colors the game made. The skin goes sunburnt, and the strongest colors hit the limit and get clipped: in this picture about half of the strong reds are cut off, so the detail in them is gone. That matters when I edit: colors that aren’t clipped I can still work with, but once they’re clipped there is nothing left to pull back. More vivid is not more correct. The whole point of the contract is that everyone sees the colors the creator picked.

Now P3 numbers read as sRGB:

Left: correct. Right: P3 numbers read as sRGB. The effect is subtler this time, so compare the neon signs.

It’s not only sRGB and P3. The video clips from my PS5 are HDR. They use a much wider gamut (BT.2020) and a different curve for brightness. If a player or editor reads them as ordinary sRGB video, they come out washed out and grey. It’s the same bug with a different contract: this time the curve (the third clause) gets misread, and the primaries too.

Same trap when I export for Instagram. The file needs sRGB embedded in it, or Instagram flattens and desaturates the image.

Profile vs space

A small point that confused me. The color space is the contract (primaries, white, curve). An ICC profile is a small file embedded in an image, or describing a device, that says which contract applies. The system reads the image’s profile and your monitor’s profile and converts between them, so what you meant is what you see.

The screenshots I work with are JPG and PNG files from my PS5. They carry no HDR information and no profile at all, so sRGB is implied, and that’s what I should be grading for.

Claude explained the rest of this section to me. I haven’t tested it myself.

So what happens when things don’t match? Two cases.

The screen can’t show the image’s space. Say a photo is in P3 and your screen is sRGB. The system still converts it, but it can’t reach the most vivid colors, so it moves them to the closest ones the screen can do. The photo looks a bit tamer, but nothing is broken.

The software doesn’t know the profile, or there isn’t one. Then it guesses, and usually it guesses sRGB. That’s fine most of the time, since most photos are sRGB anyway. The trouble starts when the guess is wrong, and that’s the washed out and oversaturated stuff from before. Some older apps don’t even check, they just send the numbers straight to the screen.

And then there’s print

This is actually where I first ran into all of this, way before I became a software engineer. I’d print photos from the Internet, or ones I took with my camera, after editing them in Photoshop. And the print never exactly matched what I saw on screen. Maybe it was the printer, maybe a color profile, who knows, it was years ago. I had no idea why. Now I (kind of) do.

Claude explained the rest of this section to me. I haven’t tested it myself.

A screen makes color out of light. Paper doesn’t glow, it just reflects the light in the room, and a printer mixes inks, so it’s a different paint box. Bright vivid blues, greens and oranges often don’t exist in ink, so the printer squeezes them to the closest color it can make. And the brightest thing on paper is the paper itself, so the whole photo feels darker and flatter than on a glowing screen.

It’s the paint box idea again, except now it’s literal paint. It’s not even a clean triangle anymore, more of a lumpy shape.

Why isn’t more bits enough?

At this point I asked the most engineer question of the whole journey: if sRGB can’t make P3’s red, why not just give each channel more bits? Instead of 256 levels of red, 65,536. Surely more precision covers everything.

It doesn’t, and the reason helped everything click. Bits give finer steps, not a bigger gamut. They are two independent things.

For nerds: the ADC analogy

This is how Claude explained it to me, in terms I know from electronics.

A 24-bit analog-to-digital converter with a 0 to 3.3 V reference can resolve microvolts, but it can’t measure 5 V. Bit depth is the resolution; the reference voltage sets the full scale.

In RGB, the primaries are the reference. (1, 0, 0) means “the red emitter at full power”, and that red has a fixed physical spectrum. 8 bits gives you 256 steps between off and that red. 16 bits gives you 65,536 steps between off and the same red.

Here is that in pictures. Every dot is one color you can make by mixing the three primaries in whole steps (equal steps of light, plotted on the same map). First, more bits with the same primaries:

Interactive illustration (dot-grid). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

More bits, denser dots, the exact same triangle. Now the opposite: the same number of steps, but moving the primaries outward:

Interactive illustration (dot-grid). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Same dots, bigger triangle, so each step is coarser. Two different knobs.

That second picture also hints at a catch. 8 bits gives 256 steps per channel regardless of the triangle, so a bigger triangle spreads the same steps further apart, and you can get banding in smooth gradients. That is why wide gamut and HDR are paired with 10-bit.

For nerds: two simplifications I made

Claude explained this to me.

The real sRGB curve isn’t exactly a 2.2 power. It’s a short straight piece near black plus a power curve, so a stored 0.5 comes out as 0.214 of the light, where a pure 2.2 gives 0.218. That’s why I say “about 21%“.

The dots in the grids above are equal steps of light. Real image files store gamma-encoded steps instead, which are spaced differently: finer in the darks, coarser in the brights. The triangle and the idea stay the same, the dots would just sit a bit differently inside it.

Why the triangle is a hard wall

A pixel is three lights added together. Any non-negative mix of three points stays inside the triangle they form, like a weighted average. To reach outside, you would need a negative amount of one light. Negative light doesn’t exist.

For nerds: the twist, you can write down colors outside the triangle

Claude explained this to me, and then we computed the numbers in code.

I said you can’t reach outside the triangle, but I was half right. With negative numbers (and values above 1), the sRGB primaries can describe any color mathematically. The greenest P3 green, P3 (0, 1, 0), in linear sRGB coordinates is:

(−0.225, 1.042, −0.079)

Formats built for this exist, such as scRGB and Apple’s “extended sRGB”, which use floating-point values. So unbounded floats solve storage. They don’t solve display: no screen can emit −0.225 red.

The real reason for the contract is that numbers eventually drive specific physical lights, and those differ between devices. A color space defines the numbers relative to known primaries, so software can convert them to this screen’s primaries and clip what doesn’t fit.

What I took away

I used to think an RGB number was a color. It’s an instruction. If someone hands me three numbers, I can’t tell which exact color they mean until I know the color space they’re in: which red, green and blue, which white, and which curve. In an image file the color profile is what says it, the label that tells you which color space the numbers belong to. Without one, the software has to guess, and usually it guesses sRGB. And no amount of bits gets you out of the triangle.

Is this information strictly required for my use cases? No. But I just cannot work without understanding the fundamentals. In any of my chats with Claude the terms pop up all the time (AI likes to be nerdy) and it puzzles me, making me feel stupid. Learning this helps to fill the gaps in my mind map and makes the conversations with Claude more level.

What I do differently now: before I worry about a color, I ask what space it is in. For my own work the gamut ceiling that matters isn’t some theoretical limit, it is my screen (P3) and Instagram (effectively sRGB for most viewers).

But this leaves a question I couldn’t stop thinking about. Why is the map that shape? Why a horseshoe, why a curved edge, and why three lights? In Why the map of visible color is a horseshoe I go after that.

Did I get something wrong, or do you think about color spaces differently? The comments are open.

The color series: 1. What does RGB 255, 0, 0 actually mean? (you are here) · 2. Why the map of visible color is a horseshoe · 3. HSL and HSV: RGB with different knobs · 4. Lab: numbers that match what you see · 5. Why gradients go muddy · 6. What “100% P3” on a spec sheet actually means

item.content:encoded:
I got into virtual photography recently: taking photos inside video games. Like any beginner, I started pushing sliders. Exposure, Brightness, Levels, Curves. Everything made my dark screenshots lighter, so I assumed they were more or less the same thing with different names. At some point I was using gamma because I was told to, and Brightness because it was right there.

My story: how I got into in-game photography

This part is personal and not needed for the rest of the article, so feel free to skip it.

I had a few screenshots that I thought were cool, and instead of letting them collect dust I wanted to share them on Instagram.

That’s how I discovered a huge community of in-game photographers. And I realized that people almost never post raw captures. There is always some post-processing involved, and everyone is trying to give their photos a certain look. I wanted to learn to do that too! That’s when I started digging.

I decided to learn editing properly, and I started digging into the tools and techniques with Claude. Very quickly I realized how much I don’t understand about digital photography. I had no idea how the tools work on a fundamental level.

Learning by doing plus books used to be my main way to learn anything. This time Claude is my main companion instead, because AI has become smart enough that I wanted to see how far it can take me. The price is that I can’t know for sure that everything I learn this way is right. For now, I am willing to take that risk.

I did look into a few books and video tutorials, but most of them are based on vibes: push this slider until it feels right. They don’t really teach the fundamentals. I come from a technical background, and I can’t just rely on vibes. I need to understand how things work.

That need to understand is how this article happened.

I think I will write another article about the whole journey at some point: the community, my Instagram channel, and everything I had to learn about how Instagram works (reels, carousels and the infamous “algorithm”).

Then I got curious and decided to measure what these sliders actually do. In this article I want to share what I found in Affinity Photo 3. Some of it surprised me.

A word on how I am learning this. My main companion on this journey is Claude, an AI, and I don’t have a textbook to check it against. That is why I measured things myself instead of just asking, and why the disclaimer below matters.

Disclaimer: I’m still learning photography. Everything below comes from my own tests, run with Claude or under Claude’s guidance, on one computer, in Affinity Photo 3, with 8-bit sRGB images. Other versions or other apps may behave differently, and I may have gotten something wrong.

You can play with every number in this article. The small widgets are real: they do the same math I measured. And if you are too lazy to read (no judgment) and just want to play with the sliders, I made a dedicated page with all the widgets and a short note on what each one shows.

Where it gets technical, there is a collapsed For nerds box. You can skip them and the article still works. Those parts were explained to me by Claude (an AI), not measured by me, and each box says where it comes from.

Key takeaways:

  • A pixel is not light. Each pixel is three numbers from 0 to 255 (red, green and blue). A stored 128 is only about 22% of the light of 255.
  • Exposure multiplies each channel’s stored value by about 1.37 per stop and cuts off anything above 255. When one channel clips first, the color shifts: orange turns yellow.
  • Brightness is a curve that keeps black and white where they are, lifts the middle and squeezes the highlights. It bends colors as it goes, and every app has its own version.
  • Both work on each channel separately, which is why colors move when you push them.
  • What I use: Levels gamma or Curves to lift a dark 8-bit screenshot. In an app with only Exposure and Brightness, Exposure for dark images and Brightness for ones with bright areas. Exposure is the one for RAW or HDR files, but I don’t work with those.

The photo, and two sliders I couldn’t tell apart

Here is the photo I’ll use in this article. It’s a screenshot from Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty, taken on a PS5 in photo mode with no filters. It’s very dark, which makes it a good test.

Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty, © CD Projekt Red. Unedited PS5 photo mode capture.

Affinity Photo has two sliders that both make it lighter: Exposure and Brightness. Before any theory, play with them. There are no curves and no histograms here, just the photo and the two sliders.

Interactive illustration (compare-exposure-brightness). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Did you notice the difference? I didn’t, at first. Both make the picture lighter, and what separates them is subtle: how the bright parts behave, and how the colors shift on the way. Yet they sit right next to each other in Affinity Photo, as if they were two different tools. I was very confused. Which one should I use, and when?

I couldn’t answer that by moving the sliders. To pick one, I needed to understand the math behind each. That is how this article started.

Later I found out that Brightness is a legacy tool. Lightroom removed it years ago (more on that near the end). But I work in Affinity and in other free apps, and they still have Brightness as a separate knob, so the question stays real for me. If you edit in one of those, it might for you too.

Two words, many meanings

“Brightness” and “exposure” sound familiar because we use them every day.

On a phone or a TV, brightness is how strong the backlight is. In a photo editor from a few years ago, it is a slider that makes the picture lighter or darker. On Instagram and in the iOS Photos app it is still there.

Exposure is a camera word. It is how much light reaches the sensor (or the film), and it depends on the aperture, the shutter speed and the ISO. In physics it is light multiplied by time. A “stop” of exposure means twice as much light.

In a photo editor, the Exposure slider tries to do what the camera would have done if you had let in more or less light. Brightness just makes the picture lighter. These two behave differently, as we’ll see.

A pixel is not light

Before we touch any slider, there is one thing that confused me for a long time: what is actually inside an image file.

A normal JPEG or PNG (and a game screenshot) stores each pixel as three whole numbers, one for red, one for green and one for blue. Each goes from 0 to 255. These are the stored values. For example:

  • 0 · 0 · 0 is black and 255 · 255 · 255 is white.
  • 128 · 128 · 128 is a middle gray.
  • 224 · 140 · 9 is the orange glow on the hand in the photo above: a lot of red, some green, almost no blue.

Those numbers are what the file contains, and what every slider in an editor changes. But they are not amounts of light. A gray with the stored value 128 is not “half as much light as white”. It is much less than half.

I always imagined the values stored in the R, G and B channels as light intensity, and I thought they would translate to lightness in a linear fashion: twice the number, twice the light. It turned out this is not the case. Finding that out opened a Pandora’s box of color profiles and color spaces that I couldn’t close again. Maybe I’ll write about it next time.

Roughly, the light is the stored value (as a fraction from 0 to 1) to the power of 2.2. That 2.2 is the “gamma” of the sRGB standard, which almost every screenshot and JPEG uses. Drag the slider and watch the second line.

Interactive illustration (pixel-light). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

A few examples, so it sinks in:

  • Stored 128 is only about 22% of the light of white.
  • Stored 64 is about 5%. Doubling the number from 64 to 128 gives about 4.6 times more light, not 2 times.
  • To get 50% of the light you need to store 186, not 128.
  • To double the light of a mid gray (one stop, which we’ll meet in a minute) you have to go from 128 to about 175. For a dark pixel the same doubling is a much smaller step: 51 becomes 70.

Why would a file do this? Our eyes are much more sensitive to differences in dark tones than in bright ones. That’s also why we all love OLED displays: they give you “blacker” blacks. A file only has 256 values to spend, so the numbers are spent where we notice them. Half of all the values (0 to 128) describe the darkest 22% of the light. If the numbers were plain amounts of light, those shadows would get only 56 values and you’d see ugly steps in dark areas.

It is a clever trick, but it has a side effect: doing math on the stored numbers is not the same as doing math on light. Adding 20 to a dark pixel (30 to 50) triples its light, even though it hardly looks brighter, while adding 20 to a bright one (200 to 220) adds only about a quarter. This is where exposure and brightness part ways: Brightness works on the stored RGB numbers, while Exposure uses clever math on them to mimic physical light.

Try it yourself. Both pixels get the same number added, and the readout shows how many times more light each one gets.

Interactive illustration (pixel-add). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Pro Tip: When you brighten a photo, watch the highlights first. Dark values have plenty of room, but light ones run into 255 and turn white quickly.

For nerds: the real sRGB curve

Claude explained this to me. The full definition is on Wikipedia.

I said the light is the stored value to the power of 2.2. That is the short version. The real sRGB rule has two parts. Take the stored value s as a fraction from 0 to 1:

  • Up to s = 0.04045 (a stored value of about 10): light = s / 12.92. A straight line.
  • Above that: light = ((s + 0.055) / 1.055) ^ 2.4.

The second part has an exponent of 2.4, but with the offsets it behaves overall like a power of about 2.2, which is why “gamma 2.2” is the usual nickname.

Here are both curves. Over the whole range they are almost the same line. Slide left to zoom into the darkest tones, where they part.

Interactive illustration (srgb-curve). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

The straight piece near black is there for a technical reason. A pure power curve is extremely steep at zero when you go from light back to stored values, so a tiny bit of noise in the shadows would turn into a big jump. The straight piece avoids that.

The curve is usually explained as a leftover from CRT monitors, whose brightness followed roughly a power of the input voltage. Encoding files with the opposite curve canceled it out, and as a bonus it spends the 256 values where our eyes are most sensitive.

Exposure: multiply the light

In Affinity Photo 3, Exposure is a single slider.

Affinity Photo 3, Exposure adjustment.

One stop of exposure doubles the light. Since light is the stored value to the power of 2.2, doubling the light multiplies the stored value by 2 to the power of 1/2.2, about 1.37. That is what I measured in Affinity Photo 3: for every channel,

new value = old value × 2^(EV / 2.2)

and anything above 255 is cut off at 255. I checked it against exports of a test image and it matched within about 2 values out of 255 (more about how I measured it at the end).

This is a plain power of 2.2, which is a small simplification. The exact sRGB curve has a short straight piece near black, and following it would give a few values more in the deepest shadows (one stop on a stored 10 would give 18 instead of 14). Affinity’s numbers matched the simple formula, so that’s what it seems to use. From the mid-tones up the two agree within a value or two.

For nerds: where a stop is not exactly a stop

This one is from Claude, and I have no source for it. The numbers come from the sRGB formulas in the box above.

A camera records linear light, where one stop is simply “times 2”. The textbook way to do that in an editor is: turn the stored values into light with the sRGB rule, multiply by 2 for each stop, and turn them back into stored values. What Affinity’s numbers match is a shortcut: multiply the stored values directly by 2^(1/2.2) ≈ 1.37. The two are the same only if the encoding is exactly a power of 2.2.

Here is one stop both ways:

Stored value Exact sRGB Affinity (× 1.37)
5 10 7
10 18 14
20 31 27
30 45 41
100 138 137
128 176 175

They only come apart in the deepest shadows. A stored 10 becomes 14 with the shortcut, which is about 1.4 times the light instead of 2 times. Values that low are almost black, and in an 8-bit file they are mostly noise and banding anyway, so I wouldn’t worry about it.

Let’s start with one pixel from the orange glow on the hand in the photo, a very saturated color. Move the slider up.

Interactive illustration (pixel-exposure). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

The red channel hits 255 before you even reach +0.5 stop, and then it has nowhere to go while green and blue keep growing. That’s clipping. And because only one channel clipped, the color changes: the orange becomes more and more yellow. At +2 stops it is 255 · 255 · 17, pure yellow. The hue went from 37° to 60° just by “making it brighter”.

The same happens with other colors, only with another channel. The teal of the pipes (this one is close to it) has green and blue high, so green clips first and the color slides toward cyan and then white.

Interactive illustration (pixel-exposure). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Now the whole photo. The histogram shows how many pixels have each brightness, from black on the left to white on the right. The small plot is the curve: input on the horizontal axis, output on the vertical one. For exposure it is a straight line that hits the ceiling and goes flat. Look at “Clipped pixels” as you drag.

Interactive illustration (image-exposure). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Pro Tip: On an 8-bit file, Affinity’s Exposure gives the same pixels as moving the white point in Levels (when you brighten, within the noise of my measurement). It’s a straight stretch of the values with a camera-style name. For +1 stop, set White Level in Affinity’s Levels panel (shown further down) to 73%, which is 186 out of 255, or 255 ÷ 1.37. If an editor has no Exposure slider, this is the same thing.

Where Exposure really pays off, as far as I understand, is RAW files. A RAW file keeps light beyond what the screen can show, so you can pull the highlights back. A game screenshot has none of that: the clipped values are already gone.

Brightness: a curve with fixed ends

Now Brightness. I was convinced it was just gamma. It isn’t, and it’s hard to find out how it works, because there’s no standard. Every app picks its own curve. So I measured Affinity’s.

Affinity Photo 3, Brightness Contrast adjustment. I only measured the Brightness slider and the Linear checkbox.

The method was simple: I made an image with all 256 grays, applied Brightness at -100, -75, … +100, exported each one and read the values back. That’s why the widgets below only offer these nine positions: I didn’t want to show you numbers I never measured.

Here is the same orange pixel.

Interactive illustration (pixel-brightness). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

What I noticed:

  • Black stays black and white stays white, at every setting.
  • It lifts the middle most. At +50 the mid gray 128 becomes 185.
  • The shape changes when you drag. Where the lift is strongest moves toward the shadows as you go up, so it isn’t a single curve that just gets stronger.
  • Colors still move. The orange slides toward yellow here too (37° at 0, 52° at +75), and the red barely reaches 253 there. The dim channels get lifted more than the bright one, so the proportions change.
  • It clips too, just later and softer than Exposure. At +25 the top few values (253 and up) already become 255, at +50 it’s 247 and up, and at +100 everything from 202 up.

Mostly it squeezes the highlights together instead of cutting them off. At +75, for example, everything from 200 up ends up between 250 and 255.

And here is the whole photo.

Interactive illustration (image-brightness). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Affinity also has a “Linear” checkbox in the Brightness Contrast panel (under the Contrast slider). I measured it too: it’s just value + 2.55 × slider, a flat offset, clipped at 255. Black turns gray. I’d skip it.

To put the two side by side, here is one photo with both sliders. They’re separate on purpose: there’s no fair way to say “Brightness 30 equals Exposure 0.7”, because they are different curves.

Interactive illustration (compare-exposure-brightness). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

One curve, three channels

I skipped over something important: both sliders work on each color channel separately. The red, green and blue values of a pixel each go through the same curve. Affinity never looks at the color as a whole.

I checked this. I put eight color squares in my test image, applied the adjustment and compared them with what the gray curve predicted for each channel on its own. For Exposure and for Brightness (at all eight settings from -100 to +100) the difference was at most 2.5 values out of 255, which is just the noise in my measurement. So the curve you see in the widgets is applied three times, once per channel.

Why do I care? Two reasons.

First, clipping happens per channel. A pixel doesn’t “become too bright”. One of its channels reaches 255 first and stops, and the other two keep going. That’s why the orange turned yellow and the teal turned cyan. The “Clipped” line in the widgets tells you which channel stopped.

Second, the shape of the curve decides what happens to your colors. Take a dark teal, 51 · 80 · 92. Exposure only multiplies, so every channel grows by the same factor and the proportions between them stay the same (until something clips). At +1 stop it’s 70 · 110 · 126, and the hue doesn’t move and the saturation (HSL) stays at 29%.

Interactive illustration (pixel-exposure). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Brightness bends the values instead of scaling them, and a bend lifts a dark channel more than a bright one. The proportions change, and so does the color. The same teal at +50 is 86 · 128 · 143 and the saturation (HSL) drops from 29% to 25%. At +100 it’s 151 · 198 · 211, and the saturation goes up to 41%. Nothing clipped there, the color just moved.

Interactive illustration (pixel-brightness). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Exposure keeps the proportions between the channels, so the hue holds until something clips. Brightness changes the color by bending the curve. Either way, it’s worth looking at a neon sign or a skin tone after you touch one of them.

One caveat about saturation numbers: HSL measures saturation against how close the color is to white or black. A color that starts just below mid gray, like 100 · 130 · 150, goes from 20% to 41% saturation at +1 stop of Exposure (137 · 178 · 206), with the same hue and the same proportions between the channels. It crossed mid gray on the way up. My dark teal above stays well below it, so nothing happens there. Don’t read too much into a saturation number on its own.

For nerds: why HSL saturation moves when you only scale

From Claude. The definitions are on Wikipedia’s HSL and HSV page.

Take max and min as the biggest and smallest channel (as fractions from 0 to 1) and the lightness L = (max + min) / 2. HSL saturation is (max − min) / (1 − |2L − 1|), and the bottom part changes shape at mid gray:

  • At L ≤ 0.5 it is (max − min) / (max + min). Multiply all channels by the same number and it cancels out, so the saturation stays put. That is the dark teal staying at 29%.
  • Above L = 0.5 it is (max − min) / (2 − max − min). Multiplying makes the top bigger and the bottom smaller, so the saturation climbs. 100 · 130 · 150 has L = 0.49 and 20%. After one stop, 137 · 178 · 206 has L = 0.67 and 41%.

HSV saturation, (max − min) / max, doesn’t change when you scale. So which model a program shows you decides whether Exposure “changes saturation”. Neither is a measure of how saturated a color looks.

Two limits. I only used color squares for these two tools. I measured gamma on grays only, so I expect Levels in its normal RGB mode to behave the same way, but I didn’t check. And every tool I measured works per channel. Tools that work on lightness only (an HSL or Lab based adjustment, for example) should leave the hue alone, but I didn’t test any of those in Affinity, so I can’t tell you how they behave.

What to use instead of Brightness

Brightness is quick, and for a small nudge it’s fine. But I don’t love that it’s a black box: another app has a different curve, so a recipe like “Brightness +30” doesn’t carry over. Two options where you know exactly what happens:

  • Levels, Gamma slider. One number, and the curve is simple: new value = old value ^ gamma. In Affinity, a gamma below 1 makes the picture lighter. Careful, in Photoshop it is the other way around. It keeps black and white fixed and it is predictable, which is why I use it for dark scenes.
  • Curves. When you want to lift only the shadows, or protect the highlights, draw the curve yourself. It takes some practice, but you decide exactly what happens. Curves in its normal RGB mode should work per channel too, so it can nudge colors as well. A trick for that is to set the Curves adjustment layer to the Luminosity blend mode, so the change should only affect lightness and not color.

Affinity Photo 3, Levels adjustment (RGB, Master). Gamma, highlighted, is the slider I use, and 1 means no change.

Try gamma on a dark pixel from the wall. Going below 1 lifts it.

Interactive illustration (pixel-gamma). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

And on the photo:

Interactive illustration (image-gamma). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

I left out gamma 0. In Affinity it turns the whole picture white.

Looking at the curves, I noticed that these three don’t push the same tones. To compare them fairly, I picked a setting of each that lifts a mid gray (128) by about the same amount, and checked where they differ:

Stored value Exposure +1 Brightness +50 Gamma 0.5
32 44 (+12) 56 (+24) 90 (+58)
64 88 (+24) 105 (+41) 128 (+64)
128 175 (+47) 185 (+57) 181 (+53)
192 255 (+63) 235 (+43) 221 (+29)
224 255 (+31) 249 (+25) 239 (+15)

The number in brackets is how much the value went up. It’s the same picture, but with three different shapes:

  • Exposure lifts the highlights the most. The brighter the tone, the bigger the lift, until it hits 255 and gets cut off. That’s why it clips so easily.
  • Gamma is the opposite: it lifts the shadows the most. The peak is around 60 out of 255, and it fades toward white. At 224 it adds only 15.
  • Brightness sits in between. Its lift peaks in the mid-tones (around 115 at small settings, sliding down toward 90 at +100). It’s harder on the highlights than gamma and gentler than exposure, because it squeezes them against 255 instead of cutting them off.

To sum it up: Exposure pushes the highlights hardest, Gamma pushes the shadows hardest, and Brightness peaks in the mid-tones, somewhere in between. That’s why I use gamma for dark screenshots: it opens up the shadows without pushing the bright parts into white.

What the other editors do

Brightness has disappeared from most serious editors. Lightroom removed it in Lightroom 4 (Process Version 2012), together with Recovery and Fill Light, and added Highlights, Shadows and Whites. I could not find an Adobe page that says why, so these are third-party sources: Peachpit, a Cambridge in Colour forum thread (people there say the old Exposure and Brightness sliders did an overlapping job) and Laura Shoe’s guide.

I also looked at LightCraft, a new open-source Lightroom-style editor. It has an Exposure slider from -5 to +5 stops (controls.rs), and no plain Brightness slider in its normal Light section, only Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites and Blacks. In its shader, the local exposure is a multiplication of the color by exp2(stops) (finish.wgsl), which is the “double the light per stop” idea in one line. I didn’t trace how the global slider is applied, so I won’t claim more than that.

Instagram and the iOS Photos app still have Brightness. I didn’t measure them, so I can’t tell you what their curves look like. I may test them at some point.

So, which one should I use?

This is what I do now. Remember that it is my opinion, based on 8-bit game screenshots.

  • 8-bit screenshot, too dark: lift with Levels gamma or Curves. They open up the shadows and squeeze the highlights instead of burning them.
  • Instagram or the iOS Photos app: reach for Shadows (and Highlights) before Exposure or Brightness. As Apple describes them, these sliders only touch the dark or the bright part of the picture, which is what a dark photo needs. I didn’t measure them.
  • An app with only Exposure and Brightness: for a dark photo, try Brightness first. In my table above, at a similar lift of the mid gray, it raises a dark tone like 32 twice as much as Exposure does (+24 against +12) and it clips later. Exposure makes sense when the whole picture is dark and nothing in it is near white. I only measured Affinity’s, so for other apps this is an educated bet.
  • 8-bit screenshot, too bright: Exposure is fine. Going down never clips, but your whites turn gray.
  • RAW or HDR file: start with Exposure. There is room above white, so it is safe, and it behaves like the camera would have. I don’t work with RAW myself, so this one is theory.

Pro Tip: If a bright neon sign turns yellow when you brighten a photo, one channel clipped. Go back and use gamma or Curves instead.

I didn’t test what Exposure does in 16-bit or 32-bit documents, so I can’t say anything about those.

How I measured this

If you want to repeat it: I made an image with 256 gray squares (value 0 to 255) plus a few color squares. I applied one adjustment at a time in Affinity Photo 3, exported a PNG, and read the exact values back with a small script. Exporting the untouched image gave values that were off by about 1, so treat every number here as accurate to about 2 out of 255.

I think there is more to find in how Affinity handles Contrast and bit depth. Maybe next time.

item.content:encoded:
I have interviewed more than 100 different people throughout my 7-year career as an Android engineer. In this blog post, I would like to share some very easy questions that I often asked during phone screens and even some normal interview rounds.

These are all fundamental stuff that I wish all Java/Kotlin programmers knew, but practice shows that still many people are not able to give a complete or correct answer to them. I hope someone finds it useful for their interview preparation and won’t make mistakes in these basic questions.

Intro

Introductory pitch

I often see people recommend preparing a pitch about your background and using it during the introduction part of the interview. Out of all candidates who I interviewed, I didn’t remember any of that and it didn’t have any impact on the interview results. So, I recommend not wasting your time, limiting the intro to just a few sentences, and getting on with the actual interview ASAP.

Pro Tip: Keep your introductory pitch as short as possible.

First impression

To get the first impression about the candidate and also help them feel more comfortable, I usually ask about their recent experience or what is their favorite thing at work. It’s a “Tell me about yourself” question, but more specific. 

Question. Tell me about some interesting or challenging problem you worked on this year.

This question allows me to assess person’s communication skills and is supposed to help the candidate relax. After all, I am asking about something they are very familiar with and should be comfortable talking about.

Sometimes, I would get candidates who would tell me that they didn’t have anything interesting or challenging in their past project. Some people had something interesting but would struggle to explain it to me.

Question. What is your best skill in software engineering? Is it building the UI, thinking and iterating on the architecture, debugging, etc…? 

Or sometimes I would ask

Question. What is your favorite type of work in software engineering / Android development?

Asking this type of questions helps me understand what motivates candidates in their work. It also allows me to choose subsequent questions, based on a person’s strengths/weaknesses.

There is no right or wrong answer, of course, but what candidates will tell and how they will tell me will give me the first impression. Saying “I don’t have a preference.” or “I am good at everything” doesn’t carry any information. If you had years of experience, there should be something you are better at or something you like or hate doing in your work.

Pro Tip: Be passionate about stuff that you do and know what you are talking about.

Technical questions

After chatting about the candidate’s experience and motivations, I typically switch to technical questions. Depending on what interview round it is, it may be more focused on coding, Android framework, or architecture. 

Java basics

Question. What are the methods in java.lang.Object class?

This question touches Java fundamentals and I use it to understand whether the candidate is familiar with equals/hashCode, wait()/notify() and finalize(). The conversation will often lead us to the topic of HashMap or concurrency or how memory works in JVM.

Other questions in this family:

Question. When do you need to override equals / hashCode? What can happen if I don’t override hashCode?

Question. How are objects compared in Java? What about arrays?

I still get candidates with several years of experience telling me equals compares by class fields automatically.

Kotlin basics

Kotlin has been an official programming language on Android for years, and many companies have switched their entire codebase to it. Knowing this programming language is not a requirement, because it can be learned pretty quickly. However, when a candidate tells me they write in Kotlin, I at least ask some basic questions to check their understanding of fundamentals.

Examples of such questions:

Question. What is a data class and how does it work?

Question. What is Any, Unit, and Nothing in Kotlin?

How can you use it all the time and still be unable to give a complete and correct answer about it?!

Pro Tip: Study the basics of your programming language.

Network basics

Android engineers often build apps that interact with multiple APIs. We have to understand the basics of networking. To check that, I typically ask what happens when you go via URL in your browser.

Question. What happens when you enter a URL in your browser and hit ENTER?

Even better:

Question. What happens when I call an API method in my Retrofit API?

I like this question because it touches on client/server communication. I especially like to ask a candidate, who mentioned REST or Retrofit in their resume. It creates many topics for starting a conversation and tests a person’s depth and breadth of knowledge. 

Depending if this is a technical phone screen or an on-site round the expectations are different. On the phone screen, I’m satisfied if we just touch on the basics. 

On the on-site, we usually go deeper and talk about reflection, error handling strategies, how OkHttp client works, types of APIs, serialization, HTTP and other protocols, data encryption and security, caching, DNS, and all the other networking stuff… 

Pro Tip: Know what happens during client/server communication.

Programming skills

Some of my colleagues like to ask FizzBuzz to sanity check a person’s ability to think and code. I find it too common and replace it with another trivial problem.

Question. Given a 32-bit integer, return it with its digits reversed. You can use any function from the standard library.

This is a Leetcode Easy problem, with all conditions dropped. It can be solved either in a mathematical way with division by 10 or by reversing a string, both of which can be written in under 10 lines of code. Only 50% of the people I interviewed were able to write a working solution in 15 minutes.

Yes, in real work you won’t be reversing integers. However, you will be working with numbers and strings, parsing data from files and network streams. This type of problem might come up during your work. Remember, I don’t only focus on the solution itself, but also on how they arrived at it, what type of questions they ask and how they write their code. Clarifying questions, thinking about edge cases, communicating well, and writing simple readable code is as important as having a working solution.

Pro Tip: Approach the problem as if it is your work project.

Final thoughts

While the listed questions are quite easy, not everyone can confidently answer them. What I often see during the interviews, is that people try to guess the answer or have some invalid assumptions in their head about how things are. As a result, they are just giving incorrect answers. It is ok to not know something, nobody is perfect. But you should be honest with your interviewer and make sure to tell them that your answer is based on an assumption or you are just trying to guess it.

item.content:encoded:
Many Android projects contain more than one module (subproject). In a product oriented project, it will be one app module and many library modules. When the team is developing white-label apps, it will be many apps on top of many library modules.

Here is what I often see in our project. When creating a new module, some developers would use Android Studio GUI and then adjust it according to what they need. Others would simply copy-paste some existing module and change it. Some people would even write build configuration from scratch. Generally, there is nothing wrong with this. But over time, this practice had caused us several issues:

  • Inconsistencies. Build configuration might differ from module to module (e.g., could have different compileSdkVersion).
  • Poor maintainability. If we need to apply some new setting to all modules, we will have to change them all.
  • Redundant logic. Build configuration may contain redundant parameters / code, developers are afraid to remove it to break something.

Since we are making white-label apps, we have created a script that automates some of the copy-paste we have to do in order to bootstrap the boilerplate for new apps. The amount of duplication in the build logic grows even faster.

Sharing external dependencies and versions across Gradle modules

One of the common things developers do, is introducing constants for external libraries. In many projects I see on GitHub, all versions and library locators are placed to versions.gradle in the project’s root directory. The file typically declares version of different libraries and plugins, and also groups all libraries by vendor. Then, all the versions and dependencies are placed into Gradle’s ExtraPropertiesExtension, aka ext.

I’ve heard that using ext to keep common parameters across subprojects is not a very good practice. I don’t know why exactly… I could certainly find some of its drawbacks if I try. However, our project is currently using this approach.

Gradle team noticed the trend and came up with a solution called Version Catalogs, which is currently a feature preview. The feature allows you to define versions and libraries in a *.toml file. Gradle will generate type-safe accessors based on the declarations in the file.

You could try using it for new projects. However, if you already have your own “version catalog” that works for you, I don’t really see a need to migrate to the Gradle solution. Compared to defining versions in a Gradle or Kotlin script with IDE support, I found it quite annoying that you have to edit *.toml. Apart from syntax highlighting, IDE doesn’t help you with the code completion (at least as of the time of writing this post there was an open issue about that), and you can easily mess it up.

Sharing common build logic across Gradle modules

Common pattern that people do here, is either putting the code into subprojects {} block of root build.gradle file, or put configuration logic into a separate gradle file and apply it to specific module via apply from: 'file.gradle'.

This is a solution, but because you cannot often split root build.gradle into separate files, the file becomes inflated. This also causes subprojects to implicitly rely on configuration logic written in the root build.gradle.

Fortunately, now there is an easy way to split the common build logic into separate gradle files (plugins) that also make subprojects explicitly declare that they are using this configuration. This approach is based on a Gradle feature Precompiled Script Plugins and this is now a recommended way for sharing build logic across modules in larger projects. Such precompiled plugins that contain pieces of shared build logic are often referred to as Convention plugins.

If you don’t have many modules, I think it’s still OK writing your common build logic the old way. But as project grows, you may not notice how your 10 modules became 30, and 30 become 50… So, why not invest a little bit of time and set up a future proof structure at the early?

Before applying it to your project, always check whether the benefits that the convention plugins bring outweigh the drawbacks (e.g. potentially slower build or some other issue).

The benefits of using convention plugins are:

  1. Just like with subprojects { } configuration block, you will be able to extract common logic in one place.
  2. You will be able to separate common logic into completely independent bits, which should be easier to maintain.
  3. You explicitly apply different convention plugins to different modules.

By the way! It is possible to migrate to the new approach slowly. I am currently implementing it in our project and have only applied the plugins to a subset of modules. Seems to be working fine.

The drawbacks that I noticed are:

  1. It requires you to use newer Gradle, as well as new pluginManagement {}, which has some issues when used together with the older buildscript. Ideally, all projects should migrate to new approach.
  2. It will take a little extra time to compile included build.
  3. This is not the default way, so when you introduce new team members to the project, they will have to learn your new “conventions”.

How to add simple convention plugin

Convention plugins are placed into an included build.

The idea is to put all your build logic into special project, which you can call build-logic. It is going to be a standalone gradle project, with its own settings.gradle and build.gradle scripts and submodules. It can then be declared as an included build in root project’s settings.gradle. Alternatively, it can also be included at build time via command line parameter: ./gradlew --include-build build-logic.

Project structure

Here is how the project structure would look like:

root-project
├── build.gradle
├── gradle.properties
├── settings.gradle
├── build-logic
│   ├── build.gradle.kts
│   ├── convention-plugins
│   │   ├── build.gradle.kts
│   │   └── src
│   └── settings.gradle.kts
├── app
│   ├── build.gradle
│   └── src
└── library-module
    ├── build.gradle
    └── src

Root project config

In root-project’s build.gradle we need to add the following lines:

pluginManagement {
    repositories {
        gradlePluginPortal()
        google()
    }
}

includeBuild('build-logic')

The pluginManagement block is important. Without it convention plugins won’t work.

There is an issue with IDEA that causes wrong gradle wrapper to be used when running tests from IDE. It can be fixed by setting version of Gradle Wrapper in the root build.gradle script:

tasks.withType(Wrapper.class).configureEach {
    distributionType = Wrapper.DistributionType.BIN
    gradleVersion = "7.3.1" // set the same version as in gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties
}

Included build: build-logic

In the build-logic/settings.gradle.kts you should have the following lines:

pluginManagement {
    repositories {
        gradlePluginPortal()
        google()
        mavenCentral()
    }
}

dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositories {
        google()
        gradlePluginPortal()
        mavenCentral()
    }
}

include("convention-plugins")

Here we define repositories where to find plugins and dependencies for our included build. We also declare a subproject that will contain our convention plugins.

build.gradle can be empty.

Simple convention plugin

Inside build-logic/convention-plugins/build.gradle.kts we need to apply kotlin-dsl plugin and add a dependency on Android Gradle Plugin.

plugins {
    `kotlin-dsl`
}

dependencies {
    implementation("com.android.tools.build:gradle:7.0.3")
}

If we would like to use third-party plugins in our pre-compiled script, we must add all of them in the dependencies block. Here, for example, we are adding the latest Android Gradle Plugin.

Then in build-logic/convention-plugins/src/main/kotlin we can create a convention plugin, that does some set up of AGP. The id of the plugin will be derived from file name (without extension). Let’s define convention.android-app plugin in convention.android-app.gradle.kts:

plugins {
    id("com.android.application")
}

android {
    defaultConfig {
        minSdk = 21
        targetSdk = 31
    }
}

Now any usage of com.android.application plugin in our project can be replaced with our convention plugin

plugins {
    id 'convention.android-app'
}

The convention plugin will apply Android Application plugin and will also set defaultConfig that we defined.

Resources

Before you start digging into this topic, I recommend reading the intro to Precompiled Script Plugins from Gradle. Then explore the examples below:

  1. Convention plugins – Official sample from Gradle.
  2. Android Sample – More realistic sample of an Android project.
  3. Real project usage

Also, I would highly recommend reading Gradle Task Configuration Avoidance guidelines. Might be useful when writing custom plugins.

Special thanks to Dmitriy Voronin for inspiration and samples.

Disclaimer: The goal of this article is to share my experience of working with Slack. Everything below is just my opinion. This is not a paid ad, and I am not affiliated with Slack in any way.

Even though Slack has become one of the most popular messaging platforms used by tech companies all over the world, I was surprised to find out that lots of teams are still relying on emails, Skype, and other conventional communications tools. I understand that Slack is not a silver bullet and won’t solve all the communication issues in your team, but I still encourage you to try it.

At my previous workplace, we initially used Skype. But as the company grew, we quickly transitioned to Slack. Not everything was convenient at first, we had to restructure our chats several times and introduce some rules to make it work for us. But over 5 years there were no major problems and, in my opinion, moving all communications to Slack has only benefited us.

In this article, I will try to give some tips on how to organize your Slack to make it work for your growing company. It might be useful for:

  • Growing teams who are still using conventional messenger apps.
  • Teams that are already using Slack but want to improve their communications.

Problems of private groups and direct messaging

I see a lot of problems that are caused by inefficiencies in internal communication in my current workplace. The company is split into teams by platform and functions (i.e. backend, web, Android, iOS, etc). Even though we have Slack in our company, many teams mostly interact over Skype through private groups and direct messages. In some situations, it takes much more time than it should to find answers or get help, especially for new employees.

Below I will try to outline some problems that we have and how can we organize communications in the company to help mitigate them.

Problem: Too many redirects

Many times I have a question about the API, but I don’t know exactly whom should I address it. Ideally, I just need to address my question to the backend team and don’t care who will reply. But because there is no public group where I can do it (email doesn’t count), I have to ask individual members of the backend team in direct messages. This sometimes leads to redirects and I have to write the same thing to several people before I can get my answer. I hope the example below will better illustrate the situation.

Example 1: “Communication redirects”. It’s Thursday afternoon, AD (Android) has a few questions about the API. He asks his team lead AH about it, who remembers, a month ago, similar functionality was done by IK on the server-side. AD then writes to IK, but he is currently working on a high-priority task, and replies with a short delay. IK tells that it was not him who implemented this API, it’s better to ask YS. AD forwards the question to YS, who came to work earlier today and is already off duty. Later turns out YS has a day off on Friday. On Monday early morning, YS replies. Because they both realized there is some problem, YS adjusted the API a bit. AD finishes his task and opens PR. After code review, the build is ready for testing on Tuesday morning.

This example is quite extreme but it has happened before. We can see that we’ve wasted quite some time on redirects here. But if AD wrote to YS first, he would have had a higher chance to get his answer on Thursday speeding up the release of the feature by at least 1 day. But how would he know whom to write?

Direct chats (and lack of public groups) cause wasted time through redirects.

One of the solutions would be to have a public chat for backend team where anyone could ask question. Other people who are also interested in the topic, can see it and will be aware of what’s going on.

Problem: No knowledge sharing

Because a lot of cross-team communication is done in direct messages, other team members are unaware of conversations (and the decisions that happened during these conversations). If there is someone else involved (e.g., iOS), we have to tell them about it later – probably in yet another direct chat. This might come up as a bug in iOS or can be completely overlooked.

We have many platform teams working on same projects, sometimes almost in parallel, sometimes with a substantial delay in time. Discussions with the UX designer can happen 1:1 and can result in some changes in the mockups. It is very easy to forget to notify other platform about the change. Let’s take a look at the following example.

Example 2. “Changes in requirements are not always propagated”. PE (Android) started working on the project first. He has implemented some features and sent them to QA for testing. iOS developer AB started a bit later and found an edge case that was not covered by the mockup. He asked designer about it, and after a discussion they have updated the mockup. Unfortunately they forgot to notify PE about it (which can happen to anyone). As QA started testing Android, they found out that it doesn’t look exactly like the mockup and returned it as an implementation bug.

Although, no matter how hard we try to collaborate and discuss questions our peers from other platform, we can sometimes forget to do it. As a result, we have to waste some time on fixing more bugs and testing them. This problem is especially prominent in distributed teams.

Direct messages slow down knowledge sharing

If all the communications with designer were conducted in a public channel, all interested parties would have been notified about the updated requirements automatically.

Problem: Ineffective onboarding

A growing company needs an effective onboarding process. And that’s not very easy to do, especially when you don’t have enough resources. If a new employee needs help, there should be a way for them to get it.

When nobody is maintaining public channels and just texts to each other directly, a newcomer doesn’t even know whom to ask, except their team lead. This puts a huge load on the team lead and makes onboarding process painfully slow.

Direct messages slow down onboarding

Onboarding problem must be solved on a process level, but this will be never. What you can do now, is encourage discussions of work issues in public channels. This will bring a lot of benefits to onboarding of new employees.

  • Public channels will let new employees learn what is happening in the company.
  • In the team’s public channel, newcomers will be able to see how their team mates answer questions – next time they will know the answers themselves.
  • Having access to the entire public communication history of the company will enable them to find some answers without bothering their peers.

Comparison of Slack with conventional messaging apps

Before I go into how exactly we organized Slack communications in my previous workplace, I would like to compare Slack with personal messaging apps. Let’s first look at “conventional” messengers.

Pros and cons of conventional messengers

There are many reasons why using one of the conventional messaging platforms (like Skype) for company internal communications might be appealing:

  • You don’t have to pay for it.
  • It is popular and everyone has an account.
  • It provides UX that everybody knows.
  • It is well established and unlikely to stop working.

All these points make popular personal messaging apps perfect tools for online communications in smaller teams. It is very easy to make group chats there. In the beginning, it would be sufficient for a company to keep communications there. However, as the company grows, the problems of these messengers will become obvious.

  • Eventually, there will be just too many groups.
  • It will be hard to search in the message history.
  • You need to manually add new employees to all relevant groups.
  • When an employee leaves the company, you need to manually remove them from all groups.
  • If you want to keep personal chats separate, you might need to create a separate account for work.
  • You cannot control user accounts (e.g., if they have weak passwords, your organization’s communication is at risk).

This list is not exhaustive, but it is quite obvious, that personal messengers are not a scalable solution for growing companies. That’s why big messengers out there all came up with products for organizations. I have never used them, so cannot comment on how good they are. I assume they all provide the same feature set as Slack and can be a good fit for a growing company.

Why Slack is better for growing teams

The advantages of Slack compared to conventional messengers are:

  • Each “Organization” in Slack manages its users.
  • There are public and private “channels”.
  • In the channel, conversations may be organized by threads.
  • Slack supports many plugins, chatbots, and integrations with 3rd-party apps.
  • It has a good global search tool.
  • You can customize notifications based on mentions and keywords.

Disadvantages of Slack

Slack is not for every company, as it has its disadvantages (compared to conventional messengers). Here are the ones I could think of:

  • Slack is quite expensive (with pricing per active user).
  • It has a limit of 15 people in video calls (e.g. Telegram supports more).
  • It doesn’t show delivered/read flags for messages (but is it really necessary?).
  • It doesn’t fully support offline mode (but neither does Skype).
  • It sometimes (quite rarely) can be down.

How to use Slack effectively

If you are convinced to use Slack in your team, I have a few tips to make communication more efficient. Keep in mind, this is just my experience, which might not work for your organization.

Introducing Slack to your company

1. Test on a small team. If you don’t have Slack in your company yet, test it on a small team first (you can even start with a free plan). Ensure that it works before forcing all employees to use it. At my previous workplace, my team was the pioneer and started using Slack first in the company.

2. Make Slack a single place to chat. As you roll out Slack to all the teams in your organization, make sure they use it for all their internal communications. They should not keep using both old and new ways, as it will ruin the transition. If all company is using Slack, completely stop using the other communication app.

3. Teach the team how to use Slack. You need to make sure people understand how to use Slack to their advantage. Public channels, threads, mentions, reactions, search, etc. More on that below.

Users and groups

To facilitate more effective communications in Slack I recommend:

  • Use the same user names as in emails.
  • Ask employees to fill out their profiles (avatar, full name, and what they do).
  • Create user groups based on department.
  • Update user groups when adding new users or when organization structure changes.

Public and private channels

Here is how I propose Slack channels should be organized.

1. #general is a channel with all company employees. Use it for company announcements or if you have a question that you don’t know who should answer.

2. Each team must have a PRIVATE channel. Private channel is used by the team for its private communications. Just like in plain old Skype, a team may want to create other private channels for CI notifications or other things if they need to.

3. Each team must have a PUBLIC channel. This is how they interface with other teams of the company. Anyone in the company must know (or be able to quickly find) a public channel of any team, read it or ask questions.

4. Theme channels. It might be a good idea to create theme channels devoted to a particular topic. For example, #office (discussing office issues), #vacations – to announce days off, #jokes – channel for fun memes.

5. Temporary channels for big projects. You may want to create temporary channels for big projects (that last for months).

All public channels must have a meaningful name and description, should be easily discovered.

Example:

Public channels:

#general
#android
#ios
#frontend
#backend
#qa
#product
#design
#accounting
#operations
#sales
#it-infrastructure
...

Private channels:

#android-private
#backend-private
#ios-private
#qa-private
...

How to maintain a public channel

To make communications in Slack more efficient, it is important to follow certain rules when chatting in public channels.

1. Keep questions on the topic. Make sure people don’t ask backend questions in #product channel. Add some guidelines to description. When question is asked in a wrong place, redirect them immediately to the right channel.

2. Reply in a thread. When a question is asked in a public channel, reply in a thread. This will ensure other external members will not be notified.

3. Moderate conversations. Make sure conversations are on a topic and professional (jokes and sarcasm must be redirected to appropriate channel). Don’t blame people for problems, suggest solutions and preventative measures.

4. Ensure quick reaction. It will all work better if questions are answered. Try to answer questions asap. If you don’t know the answer, but you know the person who does, reply to the question by mentioning that person. The team can also arrange a schedule for team members to answer questions.

5. Mark questions as resolved. Usually the one who asked should mark their question as resolved. If there are multiple questions, the channel owner team will not know which questions are still waiting for an answer.

6. Collect common questions and answers. You might see that questions repeat. Ask people to search before they ask, pin useful conversation threads/resources or put common answers to a Confluence page and place a link to the topic of the chat.

How to stay responsive on Slack

Here is how I would work with Slack to make sure it doesn’t distract me too much and I am still responsive.

1. Star important chats. To be in close communication with people and teams that I work with, I will add them to favorites (“star” them). This way, they are displayed on top of the list and there is less chance to miss an important message.

2. Set up notifications. I might set all notifications for important channels, set keyword notifications / direct mentions in some channels. Experiment and find what works for you and what doesn’t.

3. Mute all unimportant channels. I will mute channels that are not important (if I haven’t left them) to reduce distraction.

4. Reply in threads. When replying to messages in public channels, I will always do it in a thread.

5. Sort out messages in the morning. I will check Slack in the morning and try to reply to all messages.

6. Check Slack periodically. I will react on direct mentions asap. In other cases, I will check my Slack periodically to see what’s going on.

7. Mark my status. I will try to keep my Slack status up-to-date. If I’m on vacation I set the corresponding status icon and vacation dates, so that everybody knows I’m unavailable.

How to follow public channels

You don’t need to be subscribed to all the channels. In fact, what channels you follow and how often you check them depend on where you work, what you are currently working on, as well as on your personality.

Slack allows you to configure notifications for each channel individually. You may choose to be notified about any message, direct mention and/or based on a keyword. You may also choose to completely mute the channel. Use notification settings to minimize distraction and maximize your responsiveness.

Here is how I would organize my channel notifications.

  • As a regular employee of the company, I should be a member of #general. I will probably mute it though and only enable direct mentions and some keywords.
  • As an Android developer, I should be a member of a public channel #android and #android-private channels. I need to watch them regularly to be able to help my team and answer questions from other teams.
  • Because I often need to work with the iOS team on the same tasks and interact with the server APIs, I would also join, mute and occasionally read #ios and #backend public channels, just to be aware of what’s going on (people ask questions I might be interested to know the answer). I would probably also let Slack notify me of any mentions of the word “android” in these channels.
  • Depending on my current tasks, I might sometimes need to join other public channels to ask questions.
  • I would leave channels that I haven’t read for a while (Slack has reminders for that).

Conclusion

If you decided to use Slack, I recommend placing this article in your company’s public knowledge base, such as Confluence. Ensure that everyone on your team is on the same page by letting them read the guidelines. Monitor how it works and listen to the feedback. Experiment and adjust the rules to suit your needs.

The presented structure of Slack channels may not work for every company. Some of the points may seem too obvious, but it is still useful to be aware of them. I hope someone will find this useful and improve their communication.

Thanks for reading.
